Editor's note: Dan Buettner is the best-selling author of "The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who've Lived the Longest."   Watch Buettner's reports from Greece all week on "AC360°" Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis, 73,  lives in Ikaria nearly 40 years after a diagnosis of stomach cancer. Ikaria, GREECE (CNN) -- In 1970, when doctors diagnosed Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis with stomach cancer and only gave him a few months to live, he decided to move back to Ikaria, his birth island. There, he reasoned, he could be buried more inexpensively among his fellow Greeks.   But when he moved back to the island he didn't die. He has lived nearly 40 years more. And when he returned to America on a recent visit, he discovered that his doctors were all dead. The people on this 99-square-mile Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea smugly tell this story as yet another example of what they've always known and scientists are now discovering: People in Ikaria live longer than in just about any other place in the world. A recent study of 90-year-old siblings, conducted by the National Hellenic Research Foundation, discovered 10 times more 90-year-old brothers and sisters here than the European average. Why is this important? Most scientists agree that the average human should live to age 90. (You have to have won the genetic lottery to live to 100.) But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says life expectancy in America is 78. Somewhere along the line, we're losing about a dozen years -- most of them to costly and potentially preventable chronic diseases such as heart attacks, diabetes and cancer. These diseases are dragging down our health care system and account for much of the reason why the National Institute on Aging says the average American suffers about three disabled end-of-life years during which they incur 90 percent of our lifelong health care costs.   Ikarians are avoiding these diseases and reaching age 90 at a rate of about four times the rate that Americans do. They are getting the good years we're missing, dying quickly and less expensively. For the next two weeks, I'm leading "The Blue Zones" expedition, an AARP and National Geographic sponsored team of the world's best demographers, physicians, medical researchers and media specialists, to explore Ikarian longevity. We already have a few clues. Since at least the sixth century B.C., Icaria was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans as a health destination -- largely for its hot springs believed to relieve pain, joint problems and skin ailments. Our team has reviewed reports of high levels of radon in these baths and will be exploring a theory that chronic exposure to low-level radiation may help protect DNA against the ravages of aging. For much of the ensuing two millenniums, people here lived in relative isolation. The people here evolved a unique diet that we believe is a more heart-protective version of the Mediterranean diet. We're doing pharmacological analyses of dozens of herbal teas and unique honey produced by bees that draw pollen of thyme, fir and erica. We think we'll find anti-cancer, anti-oxidant and probiotic properties in these locally produced products. We also know that people here have a vastly different character than the rest of the Mediterranean. They have volcanic tempers that quickly subside. Despite living on harsh, steep terrain, they're known for relentless optimism and three-day parties. They don't get stressed by deadlines. They go to bed well after midnight, sleep late and take naps. Anecdotally, we know that most people over 90 are sexually active. Do these people possess the true secret to longevity? We're not sure yet, but we'll certainly distill a few clues about living longer, better. Ikarian wisdom may not help you live to 100. But at least they may help you outlive your doctor. Follow and vote to direct Dan's expedition at aarp.org/bluezones . The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Dan Buettner.

**Ikaria, Greece (CNN)** — In 1970, when doctors diagnosed Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis with stomach cancer and gave him only a few months to live, he made the decision to return to Ikaria, his birth island. There, he reasoned, he could at least be buried more affordably among his fellow Greeks.

Yet when he returned to the island, he did not die. Instead, he has lived for nearly 40 more years. On a recent visit back to America, he discovered that all of his doctors had since passed away.

The residents of this 99-square-mile Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea recount this story with a knowing pride, viewing it as yet another confirmation of what they have long believed—and what scientists are now beginning to substantiate: people in Ikaria live longer than in nearly any other place on Earth. A recent study of 90-year-old siblings, conducted by the National Hellenic Research Foundation, found ten times more nonagenarian brothers and sisters here than the European average.

Why does this matter? Most scientists agree that the average human should live to age 90 (reaching 100, by contrast, typically requires winning the genetic lottery). Yet the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that life expectancy in America stands at just 78. Somewhere along the way, we are losing roughly a dozen years—most of them to costly, and often preventable, chronic diseases such as heart attacks, diabetes, and cancer. These conditions place an enormous burden on our health care system and largely explain why the National Institute on Aging reports that the average American endures about three disabled years at the end of life, during which they incur 90 percent of their lifetime health care costs.

Ikarians, by contrast, largely avoid these diseases and reach age 90 at roughly four times the rate of Americans. They gain the healthy years we so often lose—living fully, then dying quickly and with far less medical expense.

For the next two weeks, I am leading "The Blue Zones" expedition—an initiative sponsored by AARP and National Geographic—bringing together a team of the world's foremost demographers, physicians, medical researchers, and media specialists to investigate the secrets behind Ikarian longevity. We already have several promising leads.

Since at least the sixth century B.C., Ikaria was renowned among the ancient Greeks and Romans as a destination for healing, largely owing to its hot springs, believed to relieve pain, joint ailments, and skin conditions. Our team has examined reports of elevated radon levels in these waters and is investigating the theory that chronic exposure to low-level radiation may help protect DNA from the effects of aging.

For much of the two millennia that followed, the island's inhabitants lived in relative isolation, giving rise to a distinctive diet that we believe represents an even more heart-protective variation of the traditional Mediterranean diet. We are currently conducting pharmacological analyses of dozens of herbal teas, as well as the island's distinctive honey—produced by bees that forage on thyme, fir, and erica pollen. We anticipate discovering anti-cancer, antioxidant, and probiotic properties within these locally sourced products.

We have also observed that Ikarians possess a temperament markedly different from that of other Mediterranean populations. Their tempers, though quick to flare like a volcano, subside just as swiftly. Despite inhabiting a rugged, mountainous landscape, they are known for their unwavering optimism and their legendary three-day celebrations. They are unburdened by the pressures of deadlines, often staying up well past midnight, sleeping late, and indulging in regular naps. Anecdotal evidence suggests that most residents over 90 remain sexually active.

Have these islanders uncovered the true secret to longevity? We cannot yet say for certain—but we are confident this research will yield valuable insights into living longer and better. Ikarian wisdom may not guarantee you a hundred years of life. But it just might help you outlive your doctor.

In 1970, Yiannis Karimalis received devastating news: doctors had diagnosed him with stomach cancer and given him only months to live. Faced with this grim prognosis, the Greek-American made a decision that would ultimately save his life in the most unexpected way—he returned to his homeland of Ikaria, Greece, fully expecting to spend his final days there. Instead of dying within months as predicted, Karimalis lived for nearly four more decades. In a remarkable twist of fate, he later discovered that all the American doctors who had diagnosed him and predicted his imminent death had themselves passed away long before he did.

Karimalis's extraordinary story is far from an isolated anomaly—it reflects a broader pattern that has made Ikaria a subject of fascination for researchers studying human longevity. This small Greek island, spanning just 99 square miles, has earned international recognition as one of the world's most remarkable places for extended lifespans. Residents of Ikaria routinely outlive their counterparts in most other regions of the globe, defying conventional expectations about aging and mortality.

The scientific evidence supporting Ikaria's exceptional longevity is compelling. A comprehensive study conducted by the National Hellenic Research Foundation revealed a striking statistic: Ikaria boasts ten times more pairs of 90-year-old siblings than the European average. This finding suggests that whatever factors contribute to long life on the island—whether genetic, environmental, dietary, or lifestyle-related—are remarkably effective at helping multiple family members reach advanced age together.

This phenomenon becomes even more significant when placed in the context of human longevity potential. Most scientists agree that the human body is biologically capable of living to approximately age 90 under optimal conditions. Yet in the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that average life expectancy lags significantly behind this potential, standing at just 78 years. This substantial gap between biological potential and actual outcomes is largely attributable to preventable chronic diseases—conditions like heart attacks, diabetes, and cancer that claim countless lives before their time.

The consequences of this shortfall extend beyond individual tragedy into the realm of public health economics. According to the National Institute on Aging, these chronic illnesses create a devastating pattern in typical American end-of-life experiences: individuals often endure approximately three years of disability before death, and remarkably, this brief period accounts for a staggering 90 percent of a person's lifetime healthcare expenses. This statistic reveals how modern chronic diseases don't just shorten lives—they also concentrate suffering and financial burden into a compressed, difficult final chapter.

Ikaria presents a strikingly different reality. Rather than succumbing to the same preventable diseases that plague much of the Western world, Ikarians reach the age of 90 at dramatically higher rates while largely avoiding the chronic illnesses that devastate populations elsewhere. This suggests that the island's inhabitants aren't just living longer—they're living healthier, avoiding the protracted periods of disability and medical intervention that characterize aging in places like the United States. Yiannis Karimalis's improbable survival, once viewed as a personal miracle, may in fact be better understood as a testament to something the people of Ikaria have long known: that the way we live can fundamentally alter not just how long we survive, but how well we age in the process.

# The Greek Island Where People Forget to Die

On a rugged, wind-swept island in the eastern Aegean Sea, roughly ten miles off the coast of Turkey, researchers have uncovered something that challenges our fundamental assumptions about aging, disease, and mortality. Ikaria, named in Greek mythology after Icarus—the boy who flew too close to the sun—has become an unlikely laboratory for understanding human longevity, and its residents seem to be doing something profoundly right.

## A Man Who Refused to Die on Schedule

Consider the case of Yiannis Karimalis. Decades ago, doctors gave him a terminal diagnosis—cancer, with only months to live. Rather than seeking aggressive treatment in Athens or abroad, Karimalis returned to his village in Ikaria, expecting to spend his remaining days among family and friends. Those months stretched into years, and the years stretched into decades. Long after his prognosis should have claimed his life, Karimalis was still tending his garden, drinking wine with neighbors, and living a life that medical textbooks couldn't explain.

His story isn't unique on Ikaria. It's emblematic of a pattern that has drawn scientists, journalists, and public health researchers to this island of roughly 8,000 people for years.

## The Science Behind the Anecdotes

To move beyond individual stories and establish rigorous data, the National Hellenic Research Foundation conducted an in-depth study of Ikaria's elderly population, focusing specifically on siblings who had reached their 90th birthdays. This sibling-based approach allowed researchers to control for genetic factors while still identifying environmental and lifestyle variables that contributed to exceptional longevity.

The findings were striking. Ikarians reach the age of 90 at approximately four times the rate of their American counterparts. This isn't a marginal statistical difference—it represents a fundamental divergence in how these populations age and die.

Even more remarkable than the raw longevity numbers is what researchers found when they examined the health status of these elderly Ikarians. Unlike aging Americans, who frequently spend their final years—and often their final decade—managing multiple chronic conditions, Ikarians largely sidestep the diseases that define old age in the developed world. Heart disease, diabetes, and cancer, which claim the lives of most Americans and disable millions more before death, are dramatically less prevalent among Ikaria's elderly population.

## Rethinking the End of Life

The implications of these findings extend far beyond academic curiosity. In the United States, the final years of life have become synonymous with decline—a slow accumulation of diagnoses, medications, hospitalizations, and diminished quality of life. This period is not only personally devastating for patients and families but represents an enormous financial burden on the healthcare system. A substantial percentage of lifetime healthcare spending occurs in the final year of life, often in pursuit of marginal extensions of survival accompanied by significant suffering.

Ikaria suggests an alternative model: not simply living longer, but living well until much closer to the end. Rather than a prolonged decline marked by institutional care and disease management, Ikarians appear to compress their morbidity into a much shorter window, remaining active, independent, and largely disease-free until near the very end of their lives.

## What Explains the Difference?

While the summary of these findings doesn't detail every contributing factor, researchers studying Ikaria and other similar longevity hotspots—often called "Blue Zones"—have pointed to a constellation of lifestyle factors that likely play a role. These include:

- **Diet**: A Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, legumes, olive oil, and wild greens, with meat consumed sparingly
- **Physical activity**: Not through structured exercise, but through the natural physical demands of daily life—walking steep terrain, gardening, and manual labor
- **Social connectivity**: Strong multigenerational family bonds and community ties that combat isolation and provide emotional support
- **Stress reduction**: A slower pace of life, frequent napping, and a cultural emphasis on leisure and social gathering over productivity
- **Purpose**: Elderly Ikarians often remain integrated into family and community life, maintaining a sense of purpose well into their 80s and 90s

## A Model for Change

The story of Ikaria—embodied in individuals like Yiannis Karimalis and validated by rigorous research from the National Hellenic Research Foundation—offers more than an interesting anecdote about a remote Mediterranean island. It presents a challenge to conventional wisdom about aging and disease, suggesting that the trajectory of decline so common in American aging is not an inevitable biological reality but potentially a consequence of lifestyle, culture, and environment.

As American healthcare systems grapple with the escalating costs of managing chronic disease in aging populations, Ikaria offers a provocative question: What if the goal isn't simply extending life, but fundamentally transforming how we age—compressing disability into a smaller window and reclaiming decades of healthy, vibrant living that currently go unrealized? The island's residents, through their daily choices and communal way of life, may be providing an answer that medical science is only beginning to fully understand.

Dan Buettner is a National Geographic Fellow, author, and explorer who became widely known for his research into "Blue Zones"—regions of the world where people live measurably longer and healthier lives than the global average. His work identified five key areas: Okinawa (Japan), Sardinia (Italy), Nicoya (Costa Rica), Ikaria (Greece), and Loma Linda (California, home to a community of Seventh-day Adventists). Through extensive fieldwork, demographic analysis, and collaboration with scientists, Buettner distilled the common lifestyle habits shared by these populations into what he calls the "Power 9"—principles including natural movement, plant-based diets, strong social connections, and a sense of purpose.

As an author, Buettner has translated this research into accessible books, most notably *The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who've Lived the Longest*, which became a bestseller and inspired a broader movement toward longevity-focused living. His writing combines storytelling with practical advice, making complex research on aging and health digestible for general audiences.

Behind every successful book, however, stands not just the author but also the editor—the often-unsung collaborator who shapes raw material into a compelling narrative. In Buettner's case, editors have played a crucial role in structuring his findings into coherent, engaging prose that resonates with readers seeking to improve their own health and longevity. The editorial process involves distilling years of research and travel notes into digestible chapters, ensuring scientific accuracy while maintaining readability, and helping to craft the narrative arc that takes readers on a journey through these remarkable communities.

The partnership between researcher-author and editor exemplifies how impactful nonfiction often emerges: through the combination of original fieldwork and expertise with skilled editorial guidance that helps translate complex ideas into stories that inspire change. Buettner's collaborations with editors at outlets like National Geographic and his book publishers have helped bring the Blue Zones concept into mainstream consciousness, influencing everything from public health initiatives to individual lifestyle choices around the world.

Today, the Blue Zones brand has expanded beyond books into documentaries, community initiatives, and a Netflix series, demonstrating how effective editorial collaboration can help transform academic research into a cultural phenomenon that encourages millions to reconsider how they eat, move, and connect with others in pursuit of a longer, more fulfilling life.

# The Island Where People Forget to Die

*By Dan Buettner*

I've spent nearly two decades chasing the world's longest-lived populations, but Ikaria still surprises me. This rugged Greek island in the Aegean, closer to Turkey than to Athens, has a saying: people don't die young here. They forget to die.

When I first traveled to Ikaria as part of our Blue Zones research, we were investigating something remarkable that demographers had noticed: Ikarians were reaching age 90 at roughly two-and-a-half times the rate of Americans, with dramatically lower rates of heart disease and almost no dementia. On an island where a quarter of the population reaches their 90s, I wanted to understand what was actually happening in daily life—not in a lab, but in the kitchens, gardens, and cafes where Ikarians actually live.

What I found wasn't a miracle pill. It was a way of life so different from ours that it forced me to reconsider everything we think we know about longevity.

## The Myth of Willpower

Americans love to believe that health is a personal achievement—the result of discipline, gym memberships, and willpower. Ikaria demolishes that myth. The people who live longest here aren't trying to live longer. They're not counting steps or calories. They're simply living in an environment that nudges them toward health at every turn.

Take movement. Ikarians don't exercise in the way we understand it. They garden. They walk to visit neighbors because the goat paths demand it. Their homes are built on hillsides, so simply existing requires physical exertion. I met men in their 90s still tending olive groves, their bodies naturally strong from decades of functional movement, not because they ever set foot in a gym.

## What's on the Table

The Ikarian diet reinforced something we'd already discovered in other Blue Zones: a diet centered on vegetables, beans, and olive oil—not meat—correlates powerfully with longevity. Ikarians eat a version of the Mediterranean diet, but even more plant-heavy. Wild greens gathered from mountainsides, chickpeas, potatoes, and homemade wine appear on tables daily. Meat is a rare indulgence, reserved for holidays.

But what struck me most was what wasn't on the table: processed food, refined sugar, the industrial products that dominate American grocery stores. Ikarians drink herbal teas—rosemary, sage, oregano—that have mild diuretic and anti-inflammatory properties. Their honey isn't just sweet; it's medicine, in their minds and possibly in fact.

## The Nap and the Table

Here's what fascinated me: Ikarians nap. Regularly. Research suggests this daily siesta might reduce heart disease risk by as much as 35 percent, likely by reducing stress hormones circulating through the body.

And they don't eat alone. Meals are communal, unhurried affairs that stretch for hours, filled with conversation and, often, homemade wine. This isn't incidental—the socializing itself may be therapeutic. Loneliness and isolation are increasingly recognized as health risks comparable to smoking. Ikarians have engineered isolation out of their culture almost entirely.

## Purpose Doesn't Retire

Perhaps most striking was what I didn't see: retirement, as Americans understand it. Ikarians don't stop working, gardening, or contributing to their communities just because they've hit a certain age. They maintain what I've come to call *ikigai* or *plan de vida*—a reason to wake up in the morning. Elderly Ikarians remain integrated into family and community life, valued and needed, rather than shuffled off to disconnect.

This may be the most important lesson of all. Purpose isn't a luxury for the young. It might be one of the most powerful predictors of a long life.

## What America Can Learn

I'm not suggesting Americans move to a Greek island. But Ikaria offers a blueprint we can adapt: build movement into daily life rather than relegating it to an hour at the gym; prioritize plants over processed food; protect time for rest and human connection; maintain purpose throughout life rather than treating aging as a countdown to irrelevance.

The tragedy of American longevity efforts is that we've tried to solve this problem individually, through supplements and fitness trends and biohacking. Ikaria suggests the solution isn't found in what any single person does. It's found in the systems—social, physical, culinary—that surround us.

The island doesn't have a secret. It has an entire ecosystem built, gradually and organically, around human flourishing. That's a much harder thing to bottle and sell. But it might be the only thing that actually works.

# The Island Where People Forget to Die

I've spent nearly two decades studying the places where people live measurably longer, better lives—what my team and I came to call the Blue Zones. Of all of them, Ikaria remains the one that changed me most fundamentally, not just as a researcher but as a person trying to figure out how to live.

I first heard about Ikaria almost by accident. A researcher mentioned offhand that this small Greek island in the Aegean had rates of dementia a fraction of what we see in the United States, and that people there seemed to reach their 90s not as an anomaly but as an expectation. Intrigued, I went to see for myself.

## The Man Who Almost Died in America

The story that hooked me was Stamatis Moraitis. Stamatis had emigrated to the United States, and in 1976 he was diagnosed with lung cancer. Nine doctors confirmed it. He was given nine months to live. Rather than endure grueling treatments far from home, he decided to return to Ikaria to die among family, in the house where he was born, and to be buried near his ancestors.

He didn't die. Not in nine months, not in nine years. When I met him decades later, he was in his late 90s, tending his vineyard, producing his own wine, and outliving the doctors who had diagnosed him. He'd never gotten chemotherapy. He'd simply gone home, reconnected with old friends, started walking to the local tavern for wine and conversation, took up gardening again, and reestablished the rhythms of Ikarian life. When I asked him about his cancer, he shrugged. It had simply... gone away, or stopped mattering.

## What the Data Actually Shows

Ikaria isn't magic—it's measurable. Studies conducted by researchers including Christina Chrysohoou and others found that Ikarians reach age 90 at roughly 2.5 times the rate of Americans. Rates of cardiovascular disease are dramatically lower. Depression is nearly nonexistent among the elderly. And perhaps most strikingly, dementia rates are about 20% lower than in the general population—many Ikarians in their 90s still have sharp minds.

## The Ingredients of Their Longevity

**The Diet**
Ikarians eat a variation of the Mediterranean diet, heavy on beans—chickpeas, black-eyed peas, lentils—along with wild greens foraged from the hillsides, potatoes, olive oil (they consume roughly six tablespoons a day), goat milk, and small amounts of fish. They drink herbal teas made from wild rosemary, sage, and oregano—teas that, interestingly, also function as mild diuretics, potentially helping regulate blood pressure. Meat appears on the table maybe five times a month. Sugar is a rarity, saved for celebrations.

**The Nap**
This isn't a myth. Ikarians nap regularly, and research—including a Harvard study following over 23,000 Greek adults—found that regular napping was associated with a 37% reduction in heart disease mortality. When I asked one elderly farmer, Thanasis Karimalis, about his midday ritual, he looked at me as though I'd asked why he bothered breathing.

**Movement Built Into Life**
No one on Ikaria goes to a gym. The terrain does the work—steep hills, rocky paths, gardens that need tending. An 85-year-old man I met, Giorgos, was still climbing the mountainside daily to check on his goats, not because a doctor told him to, but because that's simply what the day required.

**The Wine and the Table**
Ikarians drink wine daily, but almost never alone. Wine here is inseparable from conversation—it's a social lubricant deployed at long, unhurried meals with family and neighbors.

## The Ingredient I Didn't Expect: Time Itself

What struck me most wasn't diet or exercise—it was Ikarians' entirely different relationship with time. Clocks are almost decorative suggestions. I once asked a café owner what time the ferry left. He looked genuinely puzzled by my urgency. "It leaves when it leaves," he said.

This unhurried existence extends to socializing. Ikarian culture is built around panigyria—all-night festival gatherings celebrating saints' days, filled with dancing, homemade wine, and goat stew, often continuing until dawn. I attended one where a woman in her 90s outlasted dancers a third her age.

## Faith, Purpose, and Belonging

Many Ikarians attend Greek Orthodox services regularly, observing fasting periods that inadvertently create natural, recurring detoxes from meat and dairy. But beyond religious observance, what I noticed was a profound sense of purpose—an ikigai, to borrow the Japanese term. Elderly Ikarians aren't warehoused in assisted living facilities; they remain woven into daily life, gardening, cooking, offering opinions loudly at the kafeneio (coffee house), genuinely needed by their families and communities.

## What I Brought Home

I didn't return from Ikaria with a supplement or a single "superfood." I returned with a harder truth: longevity isn't something you purchase or optimize through willpower alone. It's environmental. Ikarians don't decide to exercise—their villages make it unavoidable. They don't decide to eat vegetables—their gardens and traditions make it the default. They don't decide to de-stress—their culture builds in naps, wine, and long unhurried dinners as non-negotiable rhythms.

The real lesson of Ikaria isn't found in a nutrient chart. It's in Stamatis, tending grapevines in his 90s, having quietly outlived his own death sentence simply by going home and living the way his island had taught him to live for a hundred generations before him.

# The Island Where Time Moves Differently

*A CNN Opinion piece in the style of Dan Buettner*

---

I've spent nearly two decades searching for the places where death seems to have forgotten its address. I've walked the mountain paths of Sardinia, sat with centenarians in Okinawa, shared meals in Nicoya. But there's something about Ikaria—a rocky speck in the Aegean Sea, closer to Turkey than to mainland Greece—that still stops me in my tracks.

Here, people don't just live long. They forget to die on schedule.

Roughly 1 in 3 Ikarians live into their 90s. Compare that to about 1 in 5 in the rest of the developed world. But the number that haunts me, the one I think about at 2 a.m. when I can't sleep, is this: Ikarians reach old age with about 20% lower rates of cancer, half the rate of heart disease, and almost no measurable dementia. They're not just surviving. They're thriving without the chronic diseases that define aging everywhere else.

## A History Written in Isolation

To understand Ikaria, you have to understand its isolation—and its suffering. This is an island that spent centuries as a dumping ground, literally. The Ottomans used it as a penal colony. Later, the Greek government exiled communists and political dissidents here during the mid-20th century. Malaria was endemic well into the 1950s. This was not a paradise handed to its people. It was a hard, poor, forgotten place.

And I'd argue that's precisely the point.

Poverty and isolation forced Ikarians into patterns we now recognize, somewhat ironically, as optimal for human health. No money for imported processed foods meant diets built on what grew on terraced hillsides—wild greens, legumes, olive oil, small amounts of goat milk and honey. No infrastructure for rushing meant an economy that ran, and still runs, on "Ikarian time"—a shrug at the concept of punctuality that would horrify a productivity consultant but that cardiologists should be studying more closely.

## What the Science Actually Shows

I don't traffic in vague wellness platitudes. The Ikaria Study, published by researchers including Dr. Christina Chrysohoou and colleagues at the University of Athens Medical School, followed islanders for years and found something remarkable: even accounting for genetics, lifestyle factors explained the overwhelming majority of the longevity advantage.

Herbal tea consumption—wild mountain varieties like sideritis (mountain tea), rosemary, and dandelion—correlated with lower rates of hypertension. These aren't magic potions; they contain natural diuretic and anti-inflammatory compounds that researchers have measured reducing arterial stiffness.

Sleep matters enormously here, and not in the way wellness culture usually means it. Ikarians nap. Studies out of Harvard, including work associated with Dr. Dimitrios Trichopoulos, found that regular midday napping was associated with a 37% reduction in coronary mortality. Ikaria essentially runs its entire society on this principle—shops close, the island exhales, people rest.

Diet-wise, this is Blue Zones 101 but worth repeating because we still haven't listened: a modified Mediterranean diet heavy in legumes (chickpeas, black-eyed peas, lentils consumed almost daily), wild greens foraged from hillsides (over 150 varieties identified by researchers, many containing 10 times the antioxidants of cultivated vegetables), and olive oil as the primary fat source. Meat is a celebration food, eaten perhaps a few times a month.

## The Social Architecture of Long Life

But here's what the peer-reviewed papers can't fully capture, and what I think American medicine still doesn't want to reckon with: Ikarian longevity isn't a supplement you can bottle. It's baked into the social architecture.

There is no word for "retirement" in the way we mean it. Elders don't get shuffled off to facilities; they remain embedded in daily life, gardening, arguing about politics at the kafenion, walking to church. Purpose isn't a wellness buzzword here—it's structural. You matter to your neighbors, and your neighbors let you know it, every single day.

The social cohesion numbers back this up. Loneliness, which Dr. Vivek Murthy's recent Surgeon General's advisory equated with smoking 15 cigarettes a day in mortality risk, is nearly nonexistent in Ikarian villages. Multiple generations share physical space. Disagreements happen in public, loudly, and then dissolve over wine.

## The Uncomfortable Takeaway

I'll be honest about where this leaves us. You cannot bottle Ikaria and ship it to Ohio. You cannot prescribe "isolation-induced poverty that forced a plant-based diet" as a public health intervention.

But we can steal the underlying principles. Move naturally instead of exercising deliberately. Eat what grows near you, mostly plants, mostly beans. Rest without guilt. Build a life where your value doesn't expire at 65. Surround yourself with people who will drag you out of the house even when you don't want to go.

Ikaria isn't magic. It's just what happens when human biology gets to operate the way it evolved to—slowly, socially, and without the metabolic sabotage we've normalized as modern life.

The island didn't find the fountain of youth. It simply never built the systems that make the rest of us old before our time.

---

*The author has spent two decades researching the world's longevity hotspots, working with National Geographic and longevity researchers to identify the lifestyle patterns of the world's longest-lived populations.*

# The Island Where Time Moves Differently

*Dispatch from Ikaria, Greece*

---

The ferry from Athens takes ten hours, then a winding mountain road adds another forty minutes—and somewhere in that final stretch, you start to understand why Ikaria has kept its secrets so long. This isn't an island that invites you in. It resists you, the way it has resisted Ottoman raiders, Athenian tax collectors, and, more recently, epidemiologists trying to figure out why so few people here die of anything before their nineties.

I first came to Ikaria in 2009, chasing a rumor that seemed too good to be checked: an island where roughly 1 in 3 people reach 90, where dementia and cardiovascular disease rates are a fraction of what they are in the rest of Europe and America. Fifteen years later, I keep coming back—not because the data has gotten less strange, but because the people have gotten more familiar.

## Stamatis's Second Life

I want to tell you about a man named Stamatis Moraitis, because his story is the one that first pulled me here, and because it still unsettles me in the best way.

In the early 1970s, Stamatis was living in the United States, a Greek immigrant working construction, when he was diagnosed with lung cancer. Nine oncologists confirmed it. He was given nine months to live. Rather than pursue aggressive treatment far from home, he and his wife decided he should die in Ikaria, near his elderly parents, in the white house he'd grown up in on a hillside above the Aegean.

He planted a vegetable garden—partly for food, partly, he told me once, "to have something to do while waiting." He reconnected with old friends. He started drinking the local herbal teas his mother made, wine from his own grapes in the afternoon, and sleeping when his body told him to, which in Ikaria often means a mid-afternoon nap that the whole village seems to honor like a civic ordinance.

The nine months came and went. Then a year. Then several decades.

When I met Stamatis, he was in his late nineties, tending that same garden, pouring wine for visitors, utterly bewildered by his own survival. "I still have the tumor," he told me, laughing. He'd eventually gone back to the U.S. for scans out of curiosity—the cancer, doctors found, had somehow gone dormant, or vanished, or simply stopped mattering. He lived until 2013, at 98 years old, having outlived every physician who diagnosed him.

Stamatis isn't a miracle. He's a pattern. And that pattern is what brought researchers here in the first place.

## The Blue Zone Hypothesis

Ikaria is one of five places on Earth we've designated "Blue Zones"—regions with the highest concentration of people living to 100, identified alongside Okinawa, Japan; Sardinia, Italy; Nicoya, Costa Rica; and Loma Linda, California. Dr. Gianni Pes and Dr. Michel Poulain, the demographers who helped map these zones, found something in Ikaria that even surprised them: not just longevity, but *healthspan*. Ikarians aren't just living long—they're living long without the diseases that usually accompany old age in the developed world.

A University of Athens study led by Dr. Christina Chrysohoou found Ikarian diets were remarkably consistent: heavy on beans, wild greens foraged from mountainsides, potatoes, goat milk, and olive oil poured with what looks like reckless generosity. Meat appears rarely—maybe five times a month. But the diet alone doesn't explain everything, and researchers increasingly think that's the point.

Dr. Poulain's work suggests the real mechanism might be what he calls "circadian and social synchrony"—an entire island culturally organized around napping, unhurried mornings, and what the Ikarians call *kefi*, roughly translated as an embodied joy or spiritedness. Cortisol studies conducted on the island have shown markedly lower chronic stress hormone levels compared to mainland Greek populations, even accounting for socioeconomic differences.

There's also the wine—specifically, Ikaria's native red variety, high in polyphenols and antioxidants, traditionally consumed with meals rather than as a separate ritual. And there's the herbal tea culture: rosemary, sage, dandelion, and *horta* (wild greens) brewed daily, some of which have documented mild diuretic and anti-inflammatory properties that Chrysohoou's team believes may partially explain the island's strikingly low rates of hypertension.

## What the Villages Know That We Don't

None of this fully explains Stamatis. Spontaneous cancer regression is documented in medical literature, but rare, and no one—including Stamatis himself—claimed his garden cured him. What he did claim, repeatedly, in the years I knew him, was that he stopped being afraid, and that the fear itself had been its own kind of illness.

This is where Ikaria becomes less a scientific case study and more a provocation. Modern longevity research chases molecular pathways—sirtuins, telomeres, mTOR inhibition—while Ikarians have spent generations building an environment that produces the same outcomes through means so simple they're almost insulting: sleep when tired, eat what grows nearby, walk instead of drive because the terrain leaves no other option, and maintain friendships with the same fifteen people for eighty years.

Dr. Poulain calls this the difference between "moving to a Blue Zone" and "living in one"—the built environment and social fabric do the work that willpower can't sustain alone.

## The Last Uphill Walk

On my most recent visit, I walked up to Stamatis's old house, now tended by his daughter. The garden's still there, terraced into the hillside, olive trees older than the Greek state itself. She poured me wine before noon, unprompted, the way her father would have.

I asked her what she thought actually saved him. She considered this for a long moment, looking out at the water.

"He stopped waiting to die," she said, "so he had to do something else instead."

It's not a mechanism. It's not peer-reviewed. But standing on that hillside, watching the afternoon light do something almost theatrical to the Aegean, I understood why nine oncologists were wrong, and why an island that makes you work so hard to reach it might be exactly the kind of place where people forget to leave.

---

*Dan Buettner is the founder of Blue Zones and has spent two decades researching longevity hotspots worldwide.*

# The Ikaria Paradox: What a Tiny Greek Island Teaches Us About Living Longer

*By Dan Buettner*

There's a running joke on Ikaria, the small Greek island in the Aegean Sea: "We forget to die." It's said with a shrug, the kind of dark humor that belies something remarkably real. On this island of roughly 8,000 people, residents reach age 90 at rates nearly four times higher than Americans do—and they do so largely free of the dementia, heart disease, and chronic illness that define aging in the United States.

I've spent nearly two decades studying the world's "Blue Zones"—the five regions where people live measurably longer, healthier lives. Ikaria remains among the most fascinating, not despite its contradictions, but because of them.

## The Radon Riddle

Here's what should trouble any epidemiologist: Ikaria has elevated levels of radioactive radon gas, seeping from its granite mountains into hot springs that locals have soaked in for centuries. By conventional public health metrics, this is a red flag. The EPA lists radon as the second-leading cause of lung cancer in the United States.

Yet Ikarians don't get sick from it. Some researchers theorize that low-dose radiation exposure over a lifetime may trigger hormetic effects—a biological phenomenon where small stressors strengthen the body's defenses rather than overwhelm them. It's not a prescription; nobody should go looking for radon exposure. But it's a humbling reminder that human longevity resists simple, linear explanations. We want clean variables. Ikaria gives us paradoxes.

## Diet as Medicine, Not Punishment

What Ikarians eat matters more than what they avoid. Their diet centers on wild greens gathered from mountainsides, legumes, olive oil, and small amounts of goat milk and fish. Notably, they drink herbal teas—rosemary, sage, oregano—that function as mild diuretics, potentially lowering blood pressure without pharmaceuticals.

Compare that to the standard American diet, engineered for convenience and shelf life, saturated with processed sugars and industrial seed oils. In the U.S., we've built a food system optimized for profit margins, not human biology. Ikarians eat what has sustained their ancestors for millennia—not because they're disciplined, but because the alternative barely exists on their island.

## The Social Prescription We're Ignoring

Perhaps the most transferable lesson from Ikaria isn't dietary at all—it's social architecture. Ikarians nap daily. They maintain fierce, generations-deep friendships. They tend gardens well into their 90s, not as exercise regimens but as simply *life*. Elderly residents aren't warehoused in assisted living facilities; they remain integrated into daily village rhythms, playing dominoes, arguing about politics, attending church festivals that stretch until dawn.

In America, we've pathologized aging into isolation. Loneliness among seniors is now classified by the U.S. Surgeon General as a public health epidemic, with health impacts comparable to smoking. We've built a culture that optimizes for productivity and independence, then wonders why so many older Americans die lonely and unfulfilled.

## The Uncomfortable Comparison

The average American life expectancy has actually *declined* in recent years, currently hovering around 76 years—lower than most peer nations despite spending more per capita on healthcare than anywhere on Earth. Ikarians spend a fraction of that, yet outlive us with less chronic disease, less loneliness, and dramatically lower rates of dementia.

This isn't an argument for radon spas or abandoning modern medicine. It's an argument for reconsidering what we've prioritized. We've built a healthcare system focused on treating disease after it manifests, rather than a culture that prevents it through diet, movement, purpose, and community.

Ikaria doesn't offer a supplement or a biohack. It offers something less marketable: a whole-life model built on food from the earth, purpose that doesn't expire at retirement, and social bonds that don't fray with age.

We forget to die, the Ikarians say. Maybe it's time America remembered how to truly live.

*Dan Buettner is a National Geographic Fellow and author who has spent nearly two decades researching the world's "Blue Zones," regions with the highest concentrations of centenarians.*
